implementation_notes: Nimbus JOSE+JWT carries every role: JWTClaimsSet.Builder is the claim assembler (subject, issuer, audience, expirationTime, jwtID), JWSHeader.Builder sets the algorithm and key id so consumers can select a key, RSASSASigner (or ECDSASigner/MacSigner) built from an RSAKey/ECKey is the signing authority, and SignedJWT.sign plus serialize produce the compact assertion. What replaces the classic structure: these classes replace a hand-written AssertionBuilder, leaving a thin policy facade that fixes the issuer, the TTL and the mandatory claims; because SignedJWT.verify checks only the signature, the claim validation that a SAML-era consumer performed inside its builder must be written explicitly on the consuming side.
pitfalls: SignedJWT.verify only checks the signature: a token can be cryptographically valid and still be for another audience or long expired, so claim checks are your code.
Keep the parsed RSAKey and the signer as singletons - Nimbus parses key material on construction, and re-parsing a JWK per issuance is usually more expensive than the signature itself.

MacSigner with a shared secret and RSASSASigner with a key pair are different classes: choosing the algorithm at configuration time from the token header rather than from policy is the algorithm-confusion hole.

variants.name: Dependency-free JWS over java.security.Signature
variants.implementation_notes: The dependency-free route for projects that refuse a JOSE library: serialize header and claim set with the JSON library you already have, base64url-encode both segments with the JDK's Base64 URL encoder without padding, sign the ASCII signing input through Signature.getInstance("SHA256withRSA") with the keystore's PrivateKey and append base64url(signature). Choose it only when no dependency is acceptable: you own the padding rules, the claim serialization and the algorithm allowlist, and the JDK offers no help with key ids, JWKS publication or claim validation. Its redeeming property is that the signing input is the encoded text itself, so no canonicalisation step stands between what you sign and what you send.
pitfalls: Base64.getUrlEncoder() pads by default; withoutPadding() is mandatory, and using the standard encoder produces tokens other implementations reject.
Signature.getInstance accepts whatever algorithm name you pass: without your own allowlist and a minimum key size, this path signs weaker than the policy claims.
The signature must cover the encoded segments verbatim; re-serializing the JSON between signing and sending invalidates the assertion.
